$comment: CASE STUDIES — problem → method → artifact → result → findings, with the evidence attached.
The site already told these stories, but as prose: a challenge paragraph, a
list of approaches, a list of outcomes. What a reader could not do was ask
'how do you know?' of any single number. Every `results` entry here
therefore carries a `basis` — how the figure was arrived at — and every
`artifacts` entry carries an availability `status`, because 'I built a
thing' means very little without saying whether anyone can see it.
RULES THIS FILE IS HELD TO (tests/content.test.js enforces them):
· Every claim has a basis. A number with no basis is a boast.
· Every artifact declares status: public | on-request | internal | planned.
Only `public` may carry a url, and that url must resolve — either to a
file in this repository or to a host the repository already trusts.
This is the rule that makes fabricating a link fail the build.
· No publication venue, DOI or journal is named anywhere unless the
artifact genuinely has one. Two theses were examined and defended; that
is what they say, and nothing more.
· `lenses` lists which role-specific views a case study belongs to, and
must reference ids defined in content/lenses.json. Nearest first: in
the view of its first lens a case study leads, ahead of those that
only touch that lens.
· `findings` says what the work found or recommends, not only what it
did: one to four short entries, each `kind` "finding" or
"recommendation" (at least one finding), with `text` and, as a
result has, a `basis` (required when the text has a figure). Each is
drawn from what the work's own records and this site already say;
where that is thin, the list is short rather than padded.
`homepageCard: false` keeps a case study off the homepage's cards (and
the field report, their text edition): see onHomepage in
scripts/lib/content.js. It then needs no photo, tags, location or brief.
THE HOMEPAGE CARD. index.html shows each case study as a teaser card,
generated from this file (npm run build:content), so the two pages cannot
disagree. The card takes the title, period, location, lenses,
`tags` (tools and topics; the Assay reads them as evidence) and `photo`,
and the FIRST result as the headline. That result carries a `brief`: its
basis in one line, for a card with no room for the whole of it. A brief
may say less than the basis, never more.
`photo.thumb` is the same picture 480px wide, for the card's thumbnail
(any image tool will do, e.g. cwebp -resize 480 0 -q 72).
`widget` names the interactive a case study hosts on case-studies.html:
"borehole" or "flood" (modules/dossier.js, loaded when it nears the
screen). Each may be hosted once.
`gallery` is the case study's photos on case-studies.html, in the order
shown: each with `src`, `width`, `height` and `alt`, a `caption` printed
under it and a `fullCaption` shown when it is opened larger, both carried
over word for word from the homepage dossiers the photos came from.
`layout` is "wide" (drawn wider) or "tall" (not cropped to a
landscape box); `thumb` a 480px copy, where there is one.

caseStudies.problem: Generative AI is becoming government infrastructure — but every prompt has a footprint. How does a finance ministry adopt AI responsibly without greenwashing, and without grinding innovation to a halt?
method: Mapped the environmental footprint of generative AI end to end — Scope 2 electricity, Scope 3 hardware, and data-centre water.
Built a sustainability assessment framework for concrete AI use cases, framed against CSRD/ESRS disclosure logic so the output lands in a reporting language the ministry already speaks.
Prototyped decision-support tools with real users at both ends of the organisation: managers setting strategy, and employees writing prompts.
Aligned the framework against UN SDG 12 (responsible consumption and production) and SDG 13 (climate action).

artifacts.name: EcoPrompt Coach — this site's edition
artifacts.note: Energy, water and carbon per LLM query across named models and grids, with every emission factor's source, range and review date shown in an evidence ledger.

artifacts.name: EcoPrompt Coach — the maintained tool (promptcoach)
artifacts.note: Version 2 of the Digital Society School prototype: a JavaScript engine, web app and Chrome extension (unpacked, in no store), with its own method and newer models.

artifacts.name: Sustainable AI Prototypes
artifacts.note: Browser prototypes and a Chrome extension v1.0 from the November 2025 team project; its README lists my role as SCRUM Master & Integration Lead. Its success metrics are targets, not results.

artifacts.name: Sustainability assessment framework for AI use cases
artifacts.heldBy: Digital Society School / Ministry of Finance
artifacts.note: Developed inside a research partnership; not mine to publish unilaterally.

results.claim: A working decision-support prototype, not a slide deck
results.basis: The team's browser prototypes, a prompt coach and dashboard among them, are public on GitHub as Sustainable AI Prototypes, whose README records my role. This site's EcoPrompt Coach is a separate edition, with its own code.
results.brief: The team's prototypes are public on GitHub as Sustainable AI Prototypes, with my role in its README.

results.claim: Framework tested with users at both ends of the organisation
results.basis: Public research sessions and demo days in Amsterdam, with managers and day-to-day users. Qualitative — no completion or satisfaction metric was collected.

findings.text: Between the most and least efficient model on the same task, the gap can exceed an order of magnitude, and few tools put it in front of the person typing the prompt.
findings.basis: The factor set behind the EcoPrompt Coach, adapted from Jegham et al. (2025), model by model in its evidence ledger.

findings.text: The framework came down to five design principles, among them "make the invisible visible" and a go/no-go checkpoint.
findings.basis: The printed cards in the photos below; the framework itself is not public.

findings.text: Before calling a bigger model, ask whether the demand itself can be smarter: the soft-path question from water, put to AI.

caseStudies.caveat: This work is in progress and the outcome measures are qualitative. Any figure describing adoption or emissions avoided would be a guess, so none is given.

caseStudies.title: GAIA — Green AI Assessment
caseStudies.subtitle: Method and tooling that put AI's footprint on a sustainability report's lines, uncertainty included
caseStudies.problem: An organisation that uses AI may have to report on it, and its sustainability report has no line called "AI". How do prompts become figures on the lines it has — energy, Scope 2 and 3, water — without more precision than the data allows?
method: Rebuilt the framework on published science in four modules, Ground, Assess, Interpret and Act: energy, carbon and water per request and per month, each a low, central and high value whose spread is set by the data's quality tier.
Reported Scope 2 location- and market-based side by side, never blended, and mapped each output to the disclosure line it fills: GRI 302, 303 and 305, ESRS E1 and E3, IFRS S2, CDP and SBTi.
Put one query on those lines on this site: Anatomy of a Prompt places the calculator's query on Scope 2, Scope 3 and ESRS E3.

artifacts.name: GAIA Framework — specification, Excel workbook and web estimator
artifacts.note: MIT-licensed. Workbook and estimator are generated from the same data tables, so they cannot drift apart.

artifacts.name: GAIA web estimator
artifacts.note: One page, no external requests: model explorer, scenario comparison, portfolio inventory and per-lever savings, for workloads you type in.

artifacts.name: Anatomy of a Prompt
artifacts.note: The calculator's query on a CSRD report's lines: electricity on Scope 2, cooling water on ESRS E3, embodied hardware on Scope 3 (drawn, not quantified).

results.claim: The workbook, the web estimator and the reference code give the same answers: 3,984 cross-engine checks pass
results.basis: tests/test_engine.py, in the repository, runs them on the same cases and fails if any disagrees; its roadmap records 3,984 passing at version 2.2.0. An engineering fact, not a result for any organisation.

results.claim: Each output mapped to the disclosure line it fills in GRI, ESRS E1 and E3, IFRS S2, CDP and SBTi
results.basis: The table, data/alignment.csv, is in the repository and a sheet of the workbook since version 2.1.0. A mapping of outputs to line items: no assurance or certification is claimed.

findings.text: Whose report AI's carbon lands on depends on who runs the model: its electricity is Scope 2 for the provider, or a team hosting its own; buying answers from a hosted model, as most teams do, it is the buyer's Scope 3, category 1.
findings.basis: Anatomy of a Prompt's boundary note, and FRAMEWORK.md, section 8, in the repository.

findings.text: One score hid more than it showed: GAIA 1.0 added watt-hours, litres and grams with invented weights. Version 2 has no composite: each use case's energy per request is graded against its task class's bands, with a frugality flag beside it.
findings.basis: DECISIONS.md and the 2.0.0 changelog entry, in the repository.

findings.text: Get real evidence in first: 117 of the 119 current models in GAIA's database are modelled, not measured, so measurements, provider disclosures and actual usage come next.
findings.basis: The repository's roadmap, section 0, at version 2.2.0.

caseStudies.caveat: Method and tooling, not a client result: nothing here is a real organisation's assessment. The tool sees only hypothetical workloads a user types in; it cannot read actual usage.

caseStudies.problem: Rivers carry whatever we put in them straight to the sea. How do income, urbanisation and agriculture shape the export of multiple pollutants across the world's sub-basins — and what does that mean for Africa's coasts by mid-century?
method: Modelled river export of multiple pollutants with the MARINA-Multi model across 10,226 sub-basins worldwide.
Identified the socioeconomic drivers behind the resulting pollution patterns statistically.
Built qualitative future storylines for African coastal waters, including a deliberately pessimistic 'Dirty Delta' scenario.
Integrated climate-change scenarios into the projections.

artifacts.name: MSc thesis — socioeconomic drivers of river export of multiple pollutants, and qualitative future storylines for African coastal water pollution
artifacts.note: Examined and defended at Wageningen University & Research. Available on request; not deposited in a public repository.

artifacts.name: Scenario storylines for African coastal waters
artifacts.note: Including the 'Dirty Delta' scenario. Part of the thesis.

results.basis: The sub-basin count of the MARINA-Multi model configuration used — a property of the model domain, not an estimate.
results.brief: A property of the model domain used, not an estimate.

results.claim: Identified the socioeconomic factors that dominate coastal pollution export
results.basis: Statistical analysis of model output against socioeconomic drivers. The finding is in the thesis; effect sizes are not restated here because they cannot be checked without it.

results.claim: Scenario storylines that turn model output into policy conversation
results.basis: Qualitative scenario method. Written to be argued with, not to be scored.

findings.text: The thesis sets out which of income, urbanisation and agriculture dominate what rivers carry to the coast, and by how much; the effect sizes are not restated here, as they cannot be checked without it.
findings.basis: The thesis's regression of the model's output, on request.

findings.text: Write the storyline first and let it demand the numbers: model output rarely moves a policymaker, a story they can picture does.
findings.basis: Field note 02, on the homepage, on the "Dirty Delta" scenario.

caseStudies.caveat: A pessimistic scenario is a device for surfacing what people would rather not plan for. It is not a forecast, and is not presented as one.

caseStudies.problem: Wuppertal's iconic suspended railway glides above a river that flooded catastrophically in 2021. The municipality asked: how do we keep the city — and the Schwebebahn — out of the water next time?
method: Worked in a six-person interdisciplinary team across climate science, engineering and policy.
Assessed flood risk to the city and its transport infrastructure using historical records, climate projections and GIS.
Facilitated stakeholder workshops to map the social drivers of vulnerability, not just the hydraulic ones.
Translated the analysis into an implementation roadmap the municipality could act on.

results.claim: Critical infrastructure vulnerabilities identified alongside cost-effective interventions
results.basis: GIS and climate-projection analysis, cross-checked in stakeholder workshops. Whether the recommendations were implemented is not something I can claim — that is the municipality's to report.

findings.text: Flood vulnerability in Wuppertal is social as well as hydraulic: the workshops mapped land use, housing inequality and social cohesion among its drivers.
findings.basis: The stakeholder workshops, one of them in the photos below.

caseStudies.caveat: Advice delivered is not the same as advice taken. Nothing here claims an implemented outcome.

caseStudies.problem: UNDRR needed clean, comparable hazard information to support the Sendai Framework — especially for small island states, where one storm can erase years of development.
method: Audited Caribbean disaster-loss data against external datasets for the Sendai Framework Monitor and the Losses & Damages Tracking System.
Documented global hazard information systems, expanding regional and hazard-type coverage.
Standardised disaster-reporting terminology across sources, so economic loss and damage meant the same thing in each.
Built a risk-management factsheet for Trinidad and Tobago.

artifacts.name: Inventory of 54 global hazard information systems
artifacts.note: Contributed to the organisation's internal databases.

results.claim: 54 global hazard information systems identified and documented
results.basis: A count of the systems catalogued during the internship, recorded in the deliverable. Countable, not estimated.
results.brief: A count recorded in the deliverable, which UNDRR holds.

results.claim: Regional and hazard-type coverage expanded by 25%
results.basis: Measured against the size of the organisation's existing catalogue at the start of the internship. The baseline is internal to UNDRR, so an outside reader cannot check it — which is why it is stated with its basis rather than on its own.

findings.text: Disaster risk is a data problem before it is an engineering one: you cannot reduce what you cannot compare, so loss and damage had to mean the same in every source.
findings.basis: The audit and the terminology work in the method above; the records are UNDRR's.

caseStudies.caveat: Internship deliverables sit inside the organisation. The counts are real and were recorded; the baselines they are measured against are not public.

caseStudies.problem: Freetown keeps building bigger pipes, and keeps running dry. The uncomfortable question: what if the answer isn't more hard infrastructure at all?
method: Analysed Freetown's water-management challenges end to end, from supply through governance.
Developed soft-path alternatives: managing demand, capturing and reusing water close to where it is used, and community stewardship of the assets.
Evaluated feasibility specifically for resource-constrained settings, rather than assuming a European maintenance budget.
Packaged the result as an implementation framework other cities can reuse.

artifacts.note: Defended at Hunan University, May 2021. Available on request; not deposited in a public repository.

results.claim: Successfully defended at Hunan University, May 2021
results.basis: Degree awarded — MSc Industrial Engineering, 2021. The one fully checkable claim in this case study.

results.claim: A community-centred alternative to pipe-and-pump thinking, scoped for fast-growing cities in the Global South
results.basis: The thesis's contribution, as examined. It is a proposed framework, not a deployed one — no city has implemented it, and no cost saving is claimed.

findings.text: Bigger pipes have not closed Freetown's water gap: the city keeps building them, and keeps running dry.
findings.basis: The thesis's starting point and argument, as examined; on request.

findings.text: Manage demand, capture and reuse water close to where it is used, and give communities stewardship of the assets, judged against a resource-constrained city's means.
findings.basis: The framework the thesis proposes; no city has implemented it.

caseStudies.caveat: This is a proposal that passed examination, not an intervention that was built. The distinction matters and is kept.

caseStudies.problem: The Freetown Complex is geologically stubborn — hard igneous rock where finding water is a gamble. Communities were paying for dry boreholes. The science needed to de-risk the drill bit.
method: Applied electrical-resistivity surveying to detect groundwater in hard rock.
Combined geological and hydrogeological data into GIS groundwater-potential maps.
Validated the predictions through field drilling campaigns — the only test that counts.
Produced siting recommendations for future boreholes.

artifacts.name: BSc dissertation — 'Mapping groundwater potential in the Freetown Complex: a geophysical approach'
artifacts.note: First class honours, University of Sierra Leone. Available on request; not deposited in a public repository.

artifacts.name: Groundwater-potential maps for the Freetown Complex
artifacts.note: Produced during the dissertation and used in subsequent siting work.

artifacts.name: Groundwater Investigation Toolkit
artifacts.note: Python and browser code: field data in; figures, designs and .docx reports out. It dates from 2026, years after this work: a toolkit, not this project's deliverables. Its examples are partly illustrative.

artifacts.name: Site the borehole — interactive resistivity profile
artifacts.note: A playable version of the reading the method depends on. Play it below (it needs JavaScript): read the resistivity curve, place the rig, drill, and set your strike rate beside the field records.

results.claim: 70% aquifer strike rate in subsequent drilling
results.basis: Successful strikes as a share of boreholes drilled on sites selected with the survey method, during the Team & Team International fieldwork. The site sets it beside roughly 30% for blind siting in the same geology, but no source for that baseline is recorded — so wherever the 30% appears it is labelled illustrative, not measured.
results.brief: From the field records of the boreholes sited with the survey, not a controlled trial.

results.claim: Method carried into the borehole siting that followed, part of 164 water points delivered across Sierra Leone
results.basis: The boreholes behind the 70% strike rate were sited with the survey method in the Team & Team International fieldwork. They are part of the 164 water points — 100 hand-dug wells rehabilitated, 50 boreholes constructed, 14 solar-powered boreholes, itemised and summing to 164 — but not all of them: a rehabilitated well needs no siting, and no survey siting is recorded for the other boreholes. The mapping informed siting; it is not the sole cause of the outcome.

findings.text: In the Freetown Complex's hard rock, a low-resistivity dip is a lead, not an answer: it can mean water-bearing fractures, or clay.
findings.basis: The reading the survey method rests on, which the game below lets you try.

findings.text: Collect the data before the drill bit, not after: a wrong guess is a dry hole a community has paid for.

caseStudies.caveat: The strike rate comes from field records, not a controlled trial. Geology varies between sites, and a good surveyor is part of the result.
